title: Supply-chain failures must report their own reason
description: Objective: stop two separate paths from converting a truthful supply-chain failure into a wrong one. Register item 10 of 11 from task-963cf1d125134c6193b7af0e53deeac3 (2026-08-14 product audit; verified real). Epic rail 4 applies directly: this is a wrong-reason-code defect, and a wrong code is worse than no code because it sends the operator to the wrong subsystem. RE-MEASURED STILL OPEN at HEAD 192360e, both halves. FIRST: scripts/release/supply-chain.mjs:198 `if (!tools) return releaseRefusal("FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED");` - the guard is on the TOOLCHAIN OBSERVATION, not on the frozen install, so a failure to observe Node/pnpm/Git/tar/cdxgen identities is reported as an install failure. The genuine frozen-install refusal is a different site at :211 (`installed.exitCode !== 0`), so the two are already distinguishable and share a code they should not. SECOND: :241 `finally { process.off("SIGINT", stop); process.off("SIGTERM", stop); cleanRoots(roots); }` - cleanRoots (:184) runs in a finally block, so on Windows an EBUSY from a held handle can throw out of the finally and REPLACE the real result, turning a specific refusal (or a success) into a cleanup error. Deliverable: give the toolchain-observation failure its own stable code, and make cleanup unable to overwrite the outcome it is cleaning up after. NOT in scope: changing the release verdict/publication policy, the evidence record shape, the SBOM/audit tooling, or the distribution admission path. Verification: pnpm typecheck:release plus the focused release/supply-chain integration coverage.
definitionOfDone: A toolchain-observation failure returns its OWN stable release reason code, distinct from FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED, and the genuine frozen-install failure at supply-chain.mjs:211 still returns FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED unchanged - a test asserts both codes separately so the two can never be confused again.
The new code is added to the frozen release vocabulary in scripts/release/release-subject.mjs:25 alongside the existing members, and nothing else in that closed set changes.

cleanRoots can no longer replace the real outcome: a cleanup failure is caught and reported as a subordinate fact, and the original refusal or success is what the caller receives - proven by a test that forces cleanup to throw and asserts the ORIGINAL exact code still comes back.

Signal handling still deregisters SIGINT/SIGTERM on every exit path, and cleanup still runs on success, refusal, exception and signal - this task changes what cleanup can OVERWRITE, not whether it happens.
Fresh pnpm typecheck:release exits 0 and the focused release/supply-chain coverage exits 0.
taskRails: Both halves are wrong-reason-code defects under epic rail 4: every test must pin the exact stable code, never merely that the release refused.
Do not silence a cleanup failure entirely - it must still be reported, just never as the primary outcome. Losing it would trade a wrong code for a missing one.
Windows EBUSY from a held handle is the real trigger for the cleanup half; the test must simulate a throwing cleanup rather than assuming POSIX unlink semantics.
These are .mjs checked-JS modules under a dedicated root typecheck script, not workspace packages - keep them under the per-file cap and do not convert them to TypeScript.

implementationPlan.description: TDD RED FIRST for defect one. In tests/integration/release-supply-chain.test.mjs, add a case that injects a `observeTools` port returning a falsy value and asserts the refusal's exact `reason` - which today is the WRONG value, FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED. Add a second case that drives the genuine frozen-install failure (a `frozenInstall` port returning a non-zero exitCode) and asserts FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED. Both must assert `refusedBy` is RELEASE_SUPPLY_CHAIN too. NOTE THE SHAPE: releaseRefusal (release-subject.mjs:67-74) returns {code: RELEASE_SUPPLY_CHAIN_CODE, ok:false, reason, refusedBy: RELEASE_SUPPLY_CHAIN_LAYER} - `code` is the SAME constant for every refusal, so asserting `code` proves nothing here; `reason` is the discriminator and is what these tests must pin. The first case is RED against current bytes only after step 2 changes the expectation, so write it asserting the CORRECT future reason and record it failing.
implementationPlan.note: RED recorded for defect one. Added two tests: (a) "separates an unobservable toolchain from a frozen install failure" — injects observeTools -> undefined and asserts reason TOOLCHAIN_OBSERVATION_FAILED + refusedBy RELEASE_SUPPLY_CHAIN, then drives frozenInstall exitCode 9 and asserts FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED, plus assert.notEqual on the two reasons and call-count proof that the observation arm never reached frozenInstall; (b) vocabulary test pinning RELEASE_REFUSAL_REASONS as a hand-written 20-member literal. Both RED at HEAD: actual 'FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED' vs expected 'TOOLCHAIN_OBSERVATION_FAILED', and the array deepEqual missing the new member. Asserting `code` would have been vacuous (same constant every refusal) so `reason` is the discriminator, per plan. Also added supplyInput/runSupplyWithPorts helpers so a test can hold the spy object it injected. FINDING (out of scope, DoD forbids other changes to the closed set): SOURCE_ARCHIVE_FAILED is emitted at supply-chain.mjs:61, :63, :208 but is NOT a member of RELEASE_REFUSAL_REASONS — independent proof the array is documentation, not enforcement.

implementationPlan.description: Give the toolchain-observation failure its own reason. In scripts/release/supply-chain.mjs, the guard immediately after `const tools = await ports.observeTools(...)` currently returns releaseRefusal("FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED"); change it to a new toolchain-observation reason. The evidence that this is a copy-paste rather than a decision is on the very next line, which already returns TOOLCHAIN_IDENTITY_MISMATCH for a toolchain identity problem - so the toolchain family already has its own codes and observation failure was simply borrowing the install one. Add the new member to RELEASE_REFUSAL_REASONS in scripts/release/release-subject.mjs:22-33, beside TOOLCHAIN_IDENTITY_MISMATCH, and change nothing else in that frozen set. Leave the genuine frozen-install guard (`if (installed.exitCode !== 0) return releaseRefusal("FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED")`) exactly as it is - after this change the two sites are distinguishable, which is the whole point. WORTH KNOWING, and out of scope: releaseRefusal takes a plain string and does NOT validate against RELEASE_REFUSAL_REASONS, so that array is documentation rather than enforcement and a typo'd reason would pass silently. Do not fix that here; note it in the completion for a future slice.
implementationPlan.note: GREEN for defect one. supply-chain.mjs:198 now returns releaseRefusal("TOOLCHAIN_OBSERVATION_FAILED") for the observeTools falsy guard; the genuine frozen-install guard at :211 is byte-identical (still FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED). release-subject.mjs:29 gained "TOOLCHAIN_OBSERVATION_FAILED" on the same line as its sibling TOOLCHAIN_IDENTITY_MISMATCH; no other member added, removed or reordered (pinned by the 20-member deepEqual literal). Both edits are in-place single-line replacements, so neither file's line count moved: supply-chain.mjs still 256, release-subject.mjs still 224 (grep -c ''). Focused run: 2 passed, 0 failed. Name chosen as a strict sibling of TOOLCHAIN_IDENTITY_MISMATCH ("could not observe the toolchain at all" vs "observed it and it was wrong"). Carrying forward for the completion note: releaseRefusal does not validate its argument against RELEASE_REFUSAL_REASONS, and SOURCE_ARCHIVE_FAILED is live proof — it is emitted at three sites yet was never a member.

implementationPlan.description: TDD RED FIRST for defect two. Add a case that forces cleanup to throw - inject or stub the removal so it raises an EBUSY-like error - and assert that the ORIGINAL outcome still reaches the caller: run it once against a successful record and once against a specific refusal, and assert the success and that exact reason respectively, NOT a cleanup error. This must be RED against current bytes: today `finally { ...; cleanRoots(roots); }` (supply-chain.mjs, final lines of runReleaseSupplyChain) runs cleanRoots, whose rmSync calls can throw, and a throw from a finally block replaces the return value AND escapes the surrounding catch - so a truthful result becomes a cleanup error. Note `rmSync(..., {force: true})` does NOT protect against this: force suppresses ENOENT, not a Windows EBUSY from a held handle.
implementationPlan.note: RED recorded for defect two, and the trigger had to be re-chosen on evidence. The plan's held-handle simulation is VACUOUS on this platform: I probed fs.openSync + rmSync(force,recursive) on a temp tree and it printed NO_THROW, because libuv opens with FILE_SHARE_DELETE, so a held fd does not block removal on Windows. A test built on that assumption would have passed against the unfixed code while proving nothing. Deterministic production-reachable trigger used instead: cleanRoots removes `${root}.tar` WITHOUT `recursive`, so a directory at that path raises ERR_FS_EISDIR from the exact production line. The injected archiveSource port receives {destination: root}, so a test can plant the obstacle at the real path. Two RED tests added, both failing with the cleanup error rather than the truth: "keeps a successful record when temporary cleanup fails" and "keeps the original refusal reason when temporary cleanup fails" (SBOM_GENERATION_FAILED arm). Stack pins the defect exactly: cleanRoots (supply-chain.mjs:186) called from runReleaseSupplyChain (supply-chain.mjs:241, the finally). Non-vacuity helper assertCleanupAttempted asserts the case count, that every build root WAS removed (cleanup really ran) and that every obstacle survives (the throwing call really was reached); the 2-root arm also pins that cleanup must not abandon the remaining roots after the first failure.

implementationPlan.description: Make cleanup unable to overwrite the outcome. Fix it INSIDE cleanRoots rather than by wrapping the finally: supply-chain.mjs is 256 physical lines, already above the 250 target, so the change must be close to net-neutral and adding a try/catch around the finally body would grow the caller. Make cleanRoots catch per-root, continue removing the remaining roots rather than abandoning them on the first failure, and report the failure as a SUBORDINATE fact - a stderr diagnostic naming the path is sufficient and keeps the result untouched. Do NOT silence it entirely: losing the cleanup failure would trade a wrong outcome for a missing one, and a leaked temp root that nobody is told about is its own defect. Keep `roots.splice(0)` semantics so a second call does not retry the same roots, and keep the finally block's signal deregistration (process.off SIGINT/SIGTERM) exactly as it is.
implementationPlan.note: GREEN for defect two. Fixed INSIDE cleanRoots (supply-chain.mjs:184-188) as planned, not by wrapping the finally: per-root try/catch, so a failing root is reported and the loop continues to the remaining roots instead of abandoning them. Cleanup failure stays a SUBORDINATE fact — a stderr diagnostic naming the path and the error — never the returned result; nothing is silenced. Preserved exactly: roots.splice(0) semantics (second call cannot retry the same roots), the finally's process.off SIGINT/SIGTERM deregistration, and both rmSync call shapes. Line budget honoured by writing the comment as a trailing comment on the signature and keeping try/catch on one line: supply-chain.mjs is still 256 lines and release-subject.mjs still 224 (grep -c ''), so this task is net 0 on both production files. Focused run: 2 passed, 0 failed, and stderr shows BOTH temp roots reported in the 2-root arm — direct evidence the loop continued past the first failure. The same fix covers the SIGINT/SIGTERM stop handler, since it calls the same cleanRoots before process.exit(130).

implementationPlan.note: Whole refusal surface pinned. Added a 9-row (injected failure -> expected reason) table with a hand-written literal length assertion (assert.equal(refusalSites.length, 9)) plus assert.equal(new Set(reasons).size, 9), so every row must carry a DISTINCT reason — that is what stops the new code being introduced by widening an existing guard and pins that exactly one site changed. Rows cover OUTPUT_PATH_INVALID, SOURCE_PROVENANCE_INVALID, SUPPORTED_OS_EVIDENCE_MISSING, TOOLCHAIN_OBSERVATION_FAILED, TOOLCHAIN_IDENTITY_MISMATCH, SOURCE_ARCHIVE_FAILED, FROZEN_INSTALL_FAILED, REPRODUCIBILITY_MISMATCH, EVIDENCE_WRITE_INTERRUPTED. Note the EVIDENCE_WRITE_INTERRUPTED row drives the REAL catch (a throwing readSourceFile), not a port echoing the code back, unlike the pre-existing hostile-output tests. Lifecycle: a 3-case table (success/refusal/exception, literal length asserted) proves every build root is gone after the run and that SIGINT/SIGTERM listener counts return to their pre-run baseline. Signal path: the test captures the REAL registered handler via process.listeners("SIGINT").at(-1) (EventEmitter unwraps the once wrapper, so this is `stop` itself), stubs process.exit, and invokes it mid-run against a build root whose removal throws — asserting exits === [130], the run still returns ok:true, both roots were removed and both obstacles survive. planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
WHERE TO FIX THE CLEANUP. Wrapping the finally body in try/catch is the obvious move and was rejected on the line budget: supply-chain.mjs is already 6 lines over the 250 target, and the wrapper grows the caller. CHOSEN: make cleanRoots itself non-throwing, catching per root. That keeps the finally unchanged, keeps the diff near net-neutral, and has a second benefit - a per-root catch continues removing the REMAINING roots, whereas a wrapper around the whole call abandons every root after the first failure and leaks more temp directories than it saves.

HOW TO REPORT A CLEANUP FAILURE. Three options: swallow it, thread it into the return value, or emit a diagnostic. Swallowing was rejected outright - it trades a wrong outcome for a missing one, and a leaked temp root nobody is told about is its own defect. Threading it into the return was rejected because the finally runs after the return value is already computed, so carrying it would mean restructuring the whole function's result shape for a subordinate fact. CHOSEN: a stderr diagnostic naming the path. It satisfies 'reported as a subordinate fact' without touching the primary result, which is exactly the property under test.

NAMING THE NEW REASON. It belongs to the toolchain family that already exists (TOOLCHAIN_IDENTITY_MISMATCH), not a new family - the failure is 'we could not observe the toolchain at all', a strict sibling of 'we observed it and it was wrong'. Left as a naming choice for the worker rather than dictated, since it must read naturally beside the existing member.

SCOPE HELD. The releaseRefusal-does-not-validate finding is real and tempting, but fixing it would touch every call site and every reason string in two files, turning a two-defect fix into a vocabulary-enforcement refactor. Recorded in the completion note instead.
planningNotes.risks:
THE INTEGRATION LEG MUST RUN FROM POWERSHELL, NOT GIT BASH. This suite archives source with tar, and under MSYS tar interprets a `C:\` path as a remote host specification. The run then fails with SOURCE_ARCHIVE_FAILED, which looks exactly like a real defect in the code under test and is not. This has cost time on this repo before; it is the single most likely way to waste an hour on this task.

ASSERTING `code` PROVES NOTHING HERE. Every refusal in this subsystem carries the same `code` constant. A test written by habit against `code` passes identically before and after the fix. Assert `reason`, and `refusedBy` for the layer.

A FINALLY THROW IS INVISIBLE IN THE HAPPY PATH. Both defects coexisted with a fully green suite - that is precisely why they were on the audit register. The cleanup defect only appears when removal actually fails, so the test MUST force the throw; observing that cleanup normally succeeds proves nothing.

THE SIGNAL PATH HAS THE SAME EXPOSURE. `stop` calls cleanRoots then process.exit(130). A fix applied only to the finally would leave the signal path able to throw during shutdown. Fixing inside cleanRoots covers both, which is another reason for that placement.

LINE BUDGET IS ALREADY BREACHED. supply-chain.mjs is 256 lines against a 250 target. Do not add helpers to it; if the fix cannot fit, splitting the file is the correct move rather than quietly growing it toward 400.

THESE ARE .mjs CHECKED-JS MODULES under the dedicated root `typecheck:release` script, not workspace packages. Do not convert them to TypeScript and do not expect a package-filtered pnpm leg to cover them.
